claims.claim: The results add to concerns regarding the use of anti-PrP antibodies as therapeutic tools for treatment of prion diseases and Alzheimer's disease, given the potential side-effects of these reagents on neuronal viability at nanomolar concentrations.
claims.source: First, they add to concerns that have been raised regarding the use of anti-PrP antibodies as therapeutic tools for treatment of prion diseases (White et al., 2003) and Alzheimer's disease (Klyubin et al., 2014), given the potential side-effects of these reagents on neuronal viability at nanomolar concentrations (Reimann et al., 2016; Solforosi et al., 2004; Sonati et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citations to prior studies (White et al., 2003; Klyubin et al., 2014; Reimann et al., 2016; Solforosi et al., 2004; Sonati et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Pathologic ligands that bind to PrPC could produce neurotoxic effects by disrupting the normal regulatory cis-interaction between the N- and C-terminal domains.
claims.source: Second, our results also suggest a mechanism by which pathologic ligands that bind to PrPC could produce neurotoxic effects by disrupting the normal regulatory cis-interaction between the N- and C-terminal domains, similar to the action of the antibodies described in this study.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The Alzheimer's Aβ peptide binds to PrPC and triggers functional and structural alterations in synaptic transmission.
claims.source: The Alzheimer's Aβ peptide, which binds to PrPC and triggers functional and structural alterations in synaptic transmission (Laurén et al., 2009), is an example of such a ligand.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laurén et al., 2009.

claims.claim: PrPSc binds to PrPC.
claims.source: PrPSc, which also binds to PrPC (Solforosi et al., 2007), might act in a similar fashion, although the fact that mice expressing N-terminally truncated PrPC remain susceptible to prion diseases (Supattapone et al., 2001; Turnbaugh et al., 2012) argues against this as the primary pathogenic mechanism in these disorders.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Solforosi et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Mice expressing N-terminally truncated PrPC remain susceptible to prion diseases.
claims.source: PrPSc, which also binds to PrPC (Solforosi et al., 2007), might act in a similar fashion, although the fact that mice expressing N-terminally truncated PrPC remain susceptible to prion diseases (Supattapone et al., 2001; Turnbaugh et al., 2012) argues against this as the primary pathogenic mechanism in these disorders.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Supattapone et al., 2001 and Turnbaugh et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Natural ligands, including proteins, small molecules or metal ions, may exist, whose binding to PrPC regulates an effector activity of the N-terminal domain.
claims.source: If so, natural ligands, including proteins, small molecules or metal ions, may exist, whose binding to PrPC regulates an effector activity of the N-terminal domain, similar to the way that we suppose anti-PrP antibodies operate.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Copper ions are examples of natural ligands, binding of which to the octapeptide repeats promotes docking of the N- and C-terminal domains.
claims.source: Copper ions are examples of natural ligands, binding of which to the octapeptide repeats promotes docking of the N- and C-terminal domains (Evans et al., 2016; Spevacek et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Evans et al., 2016 and Spevacek et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Previous studies have implicated the N-terminal domain of PrPC in several physiological activities of PrPC.
claims.source: Previous studies have implicated the N-terminal domain of PrPC in several physiological activities of PrPC (Parkin et al., 2007; Pauly and Harris, 1998; Sempou et al., 2016; Shyng et al., 1995b; Taylor et al., 2005; Watt et al., 2012), some of which may be regulated by interaction with the C-terminal domain.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Parkin et al., 2007; Pauly and Harris, 1998; Sempou et al., 2016; Shyng et al., 1995b; Taylor et al., 2005; Watt et al., 2012).

results.result: The N-terminal domain of PrPC functions as a toxic effector whose activity is regulated in cis by the C-terminal domain. This represents a novel auto-inhibitory mechanism controlling PrPC function.
results.evaluation: This central mechanistic model is well-supported by convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches (electrophysiology, cellular assays, NMR). Claims C2-C3 and C69-C70 are directly supported by experimental data showing that the isolated N-terminus induces currents and that basic residues are essential. Claim C10 integrates NMR and functional data to propose the auto-inhibitory mechanism, which is a reasonable inference from the presented evidence.

results.result: N-terminal ligands (antibodies 100B3 and POM11, pentosan polysulfate, Cu2+ ions) and charge reversal mutations abolish ΔCR PrP-induced spontaneous ionic currents without altering protein localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C26 are directly supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figures 1 and supplements, with appropriate statistical analysis (n=10, p<0.05). Claims C27 and C30 are reasonable inferences from the data. Claim C28 is supported by immunofluorescence controls showing no acute trafficking changes. Claim C29 demonstrates the importance of positive charges through charge-reversal mutagenesis.

results.result: The isolated N-terminal domain of PrPC, when fused to EGFP-GPI, induces spontaneous ionic currents that are dependent on residues 23-31, blocked by N-terminal ligands, suppressed by wild-type PrP co-expression, and voltage-dependent.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C38 are well-supported by patch-clamp recordings from cells expressing PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI constructs (Figure 2 and supplements). The data show length-dependent current activity (C32), dependence on the 23-31 region (C33), and parallel properties to ΔCR currents. Statistical analysis is provided (n=5-10, p<0.05). The C-terminal domain alone produces no currents (C34), providing an important negative control.

results.result: NMR experiments demonstrate Cu2+-promoted intramolecular docking between the N-terminal octapeptide repeats and a C-terminal surface encompassing helices 2 and 3. This interaction is weakened in ΔCR PrP.
results.evaluation: Claims C39 and C78-C79 cite prior NMR work (Evans et al., 2016; Spevacek et al., 2013) establishing N-C domain interaction. Claim C80 is supported by new 1H-15N HSQC NMR data (Figure 3) showing reduced paramagnetic relaxation enhancement in ΔCR compared to wild-type, indicating weakened Cu2+-induced N-C interaction. Claims C40 and C77 are reasonable inferences integrating NMR and functional data.

results.result: Antibodies targeting helix 1 in the C-terminal domain (POM1, D18, ICSM-18) induce spontaneous ionic currents in cells expressing wild-type PrPC. These currents are identical to ΔCR currents, depend on the N-terminal domain, and are not due to antibody cross-linking or Fc-mediated effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C51 are supported by extensive patch-clamp data (Figure 4 and supplements) with appropriate controls including PrP-null cells (C48), PIPLC treatment (C47), and Fab/scFv fragments (C50-C51). Statistical significance is demonstrated (n=5-20, p<0.01-0.005). Claim C77 proposing that antibodies disrupt N-C interaction is a reasonable mechanistic inference supported by the epitope mapping (C76) and functional data.

results.result: Antibody epitope specificity determines current-inducing activity: antibodies targeting helix 1 are most potent, those targeting residues 93-109 show weak or no activity, and those targeting other C-terminal epitopes are inactive.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 are supported by systematic testing of multiple antibodies with different epitopes (Figure 4 supplements 3-4). The data show clear epitope-dependent differences in current induction, with helix 1 antibodies being most effective. Sample sizes are adequate (n=10) and the pattern is consistent across multiple antibodies.

results.result: Antibody D18 induces spontaneous currents in hippocampal neurons from PrP-overexpressing mice but not from PrP-knockout mice, demonstrating PrP-dependence in primary neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 are supported by patch-clamp recordings from primary hippocampal neurons (Figure 4 supplement 5). The PrP-knockout control (C57) is essential and demonstrates specificity. The increased neuronal fragility noted in C56 is an important observation, though the mechanism is not fully elucidated.

results.result: Antibodies POM1 and D18 cause dendritic beading in hippocampal neurons in a PrP expression level-dependent manner. This effect correlates with antibody potency in inducing currents and is absent with non-specific IgG or non-current-inducing antibodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63 are supported by morphological analysis of MAP2-stained neurons (Figure 5 and supplements) with quantification from multiple cultures (n=10 images, 3 cultures). The PrP-dependence (C59), negative controls (C60), and correlation with current-inducing activity (C61-C63) strengthen the conclusions. Statistical significance is demonstrated (p<0.01-0.005).

results.result: Antibody-induced dendritic degeneration is entirely dependent on the N-terminal domain of PrPC and is blocked by N-terminal ligands (PPS, 100B3, POM11).
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 and C82 are supported by experiments using neurons from mice expressing N-terminally deleted PrP (Figure 6) and co-treatment with N-terminal ligands (Figure 5B-D). The parallel between current inhibition and dendrotoxicity blockade strengthens the mechanistic link. Quantitative data with statistical analysis are provided.

results.result: ICSM-18 antibody (both holo-antibody and scFv) causes dendritic beading and neuronal loss in a PrP-dependent manner, with effects observed at nanomolar concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by morphological analysis (Figure 7) showing dose-dependent effects and PrP-dependence. The scFv data (C68) demonstrate that the effect is not due to antibody cross-linking. Statistical analysis is provided (n=10 images, 3 cultures, p<0.005). This has important implications for therapeutic antibody development.

results.result: Chronic antibody treatment causes dendritic morphological changes that may be mechanistically linked to ionic current activity, potentially through excitotoxic pathways.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 is supported by experimental data showing dendritic changes after 48-hour antibody treatment. However, claims C83-C84 are speculative regarding the mechanistic connection between currents and dendritic degeneration. While the correlation is strong and the glutamate excitotoxicity hypothesis is plausible (supported by citations), direct causal evidence is lacking. Additional experiments would be needed to establish the mechanism definitively.

results.result: Wild-type PrP suppresses ionic currents induced by ΔCR and PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI in a dose-dependent manner, and this suppression requires the 23-31 region.
results.evaluation: Claims C16, C19, C36, and C74 are supported by co-expression experiments showing dose-dependent current suppression (Figure 2 supplement 1C-D). Claim C37 demonstrates that the 23-31 region is required for suppression, consistent with in vivo rescue data (cited from Turnbaugh et al., 2011). This suggests competition for a common target or direct interaction between wild-type and mutant forms.

results.result: The polybasic region (residues 23-31) resembles a protein transduction domain capable of penetrating lipid bilayers, and current activity is observed only at hyperpolarized potentials similar to neuronal resting potential.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 cite relevant literature on protein transduction domains. Claim C73 is supported by voltage-clamp data (Figure 2 supplement 1G-H) showing voltage-dependence of currents. This provides a plausible mechanistic model, though direct evidence of membrane penetration is not provided. The voltage-dependence is consistent with the proposed mechanism.

results.result: The findings have important implications for the safety of anti-PrP antibody therapies and suggest that pathologic ligands could produce neurotoxicity by disrupting N-C domain interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 are reasonable inferences from the experimental data showing antibody-induced currents and neurotoxicity at nanomolar concentrations. The therapeutic implications (C90) are supported by the ICSM-18 data and citations to proposed clinical applications. Claim C91 regarding pathologic ligands is speculative but logically follows from the demonstrated mechanism. These are appropriate discussion points rather than primary experimental findings.

results.result: Background context: PrPC transduces PrPSc neurotoxicity, consists of N-terminal and C-terminal domains, and deletions in the central region (particularly ΔCR) cause spontaneous neurodegenerative phenotypes associated with ionic currents.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C11-C15, C17-C18 are supported by citations to prior literature establishing the field context. Claim C20 is an inference from the correlation between currents and neurotoxicity. These claims provide essential background but are not novel findings of this study. They appropriately frame the research questions addressed by the manuscript.

results.result: Prior studies have reported conflicting results regarding the neurotoxicity of anti-PrP antibodies in vivo and in brain slices, with some showing acute neuronal death and others showing no toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. The conflicting results in the literature (C85 vs C86) are noted, which provides important context for the current findings. These claims establish the rationale for the current study's approach using cultured neurons and shorter treatment times.

results.result: Discussion of potential physiological and pathological ligands: Aβ peptide and PrPSc bind PrPC and could disrupt N-C interactions, though N-terminal truncation studies argue against this as the primary prion disease mechanism. Natural ligands including copper ions may regulate N-terminal effector activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 cite relevant literature on Aβ and PrPSc binding to PrPC. Claims C95-C97 are speculative regarding natural ligands and physiological regulation. While C96 on copper is supported by citations, the broader speculation about unknown natural ligands (C95) and physiological activities (C97) lacks direct experimental support in this manuscript. These are appropriate discussion points but represent hypotheses for future work.
